title: Machine interface
text:
Use proj --machine <command> for automation. Human command output remains the default. proj capabilities (also with --machine) reports protocol/capability versions and supported command families without loading a project.
Protocol version 1 writes one JSON object and a newline to stdout. Both success and failure include protocol_version, cli_version, ok, result, and error. result is null on failure; error is null on success. Failures exit nonzero. Broken output pipes cannot receive a complete object and also exit nonzero.
proj --machine capabilities
proj --machine --project . path get --label output
proj --machine --project . version get
proj --machine --project . yml read
proj --machine --project . build-dev
Successful queries return { "path": "..." }, { "version": { "major": 1, "minor": 2, "patch": 3, "dev": 0 }, "text": "v1.2.3" }, or { "validated": true }. Configuration queries validate without returning raw configuration or parameter values. Other existing command families reuse the ordinary CLI in a noninteractive subprocess and return { "completed": true } only when that command succeeds. Unsupported command arguments fail; capability flags explicitly report absent preview isolation, attempt/release records and direct R/IDE parity.
Stable error codes are invalid_arguments, project_selection_failed, query_failed, command_failed, and worker_unavailable. Messages are static; raw config, environment values, command arguments and chained domain errors are not copied into protocol errors. This transport reuses existing anyhow domain handling tracked by issue87; it does not promise a finer domain-error taxonomy. With --machine, help/version display requests return capability negotiation.
All command progress and child stdout/stderr go to stderr, streamed directly without accumulating logs in memory. Machine mode closes child stdin and enables noninteractive policy. Child logs are user/third-party output and are not a secret redaction service; avoid printing credentials in scripts. No environment/config dump is included in the machine result. Callers must keep stdout and stderr separate.
A failed publication can follow successful local analysis. command_failed is not a rollback or retry instruction: inspect local state/diagnostics before retrying. No analysis-free publication retry or successful release record is invented here.


Current source adds remote versions to capability negotiation, independently of the installed preview. Its successful result is an object containing versions, an array ordered newest-first for archive layouts. Each entry contains version (a leading-v numeric string), path (the actual physical directory), empty and present booleans, and metadata_untrusted (the latest VERSION asterisk boolean, or null for archives). An empty result is versions: [].
Present means a real directory exists, not that its contents match metadata. Neither false nor null metadata_untrusted proves integrity. Failed queries use query_failed without returning the raw path or filesystem error. See the command reference for layout and missing-target semantics.
The mutating remote download command follows the existing noninteractive worker route, returning completed: true on success and command_failed on failure. See its command reference for the explicit destination and bounded recovery contract; a failed post-install cleanup is not an instruction to repeat blindly.
Current source adds remote store –dry-run as a read-only plan query. Its result contains plan with source, destination, strategy, uploads, overwrites, removals, same_bytes and applied=false. Normal remote store uses the existing worker route and returns completed:true only after success. This file-policy command does not publish remote metadata or load configured source/destination policy.

Each entry contains version (a leading-v numeric string), path (the actual physical directory), empty and present booleans, and metadata_untrusted (the latest VERSION asterisk boolean, or null for archives). An empty result is versions: [].
Present means a real directory exists, not that its contents match metadata. Neither false nor null metadata_untrusted proves integrity. Failed queries use query_failed without returning the raw path or filesystem error. See the command reference for layout and missing-target semantics.
The mutating remote download command follows the existing noninteractive worker route, returning completed: true on success and command_failed on failure. See its command reference for the explicit destination and bounded recovery contract; a failed post-install cleanup is not an instruction to repeat blindly.
Current source adds remote store –dry-run as a read-only plan query. Its result contains plan with source, destination, strategy, uploads, overwrites, removals, same_bytes and applied=false. Normal remote store uses the existing worker route and returns completed:true only after success. This file-policy command does not publish remote metadata or load configured source/destination policy.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
text:
Available in preview.5. The Xet option remains experimental and requires its separate pinned helper. Keep independent backups.
Use Xet when large changed files share repeated pieces of bytes. Choose ordinary backups or whole-file sharing when chunk sharing is unnecessary. The helper is optional and separate from the CLI and R package.
Files are split into reusable pieces by the optional upstream Xet helper. This may save storage when large files share uncompressed bytes. Already-compressed files may benefit little. Synthetic results do not predict savings for real datasets.
Both local and GitHub destinations use structure: xet. GitHub transports this same local engine/store as a complete ZIP, not a hosted Xet service. One long-running storage release holds it. No incremental pack transport or automatic migration is implemented. Tests use synthetic bytes; existing user datasets are not uploaded by the test workflow.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
text:
Install the optional helper
The helper is qualified on Linux/WSL. A macOS helper has not been qualified; native Windows Xet execution is rejected. Other storage backends remain available on Windows. The normal CLI download needs no Rust compiler, but building this optional helper needs Python 3, Git, a native C/C++ compiler/linker and CMake, Rust/Cargo 1.95.0 with Clippy, and network access to pinned source and locked registry dependencies.
From the matching projcli source checkout:
rustup toolchain install 1.95.0 --component clippy
work=$(mktemp -d)
python3 tools/xet-engine/build.py \
  --source "$work/upstream" \
  --output "$HOME/.local/bin/proj-xet-engine"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
proj-xet-engine info
The source directory must not already exist. This substantial optional build fetches the exact upstream pin into that disposable directory, checks Cargo.lock, builds and lints the helper, and writes provenance beside it. It does not modify the original projr checkout or require a Hugging Face account/server. Keep the provenance with your store; no automatic helper upgrade occurs.

text:
Choose the storage options

manifest

Local and GitHub examples below archive existing raw-data with scripts: [] and Git disabled. Use explicit paths and an existing VERSION file. Preview first; the production build updates version and saves selected data:
proj build-dev

Since these examples disable Git integration, commit .proj/remotes references alongside VERSION/configuration yourself if you need recovery from a future checkout. Removing a destination from build.dest stops uploads without removing restore access.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
text:
Why this remains experimental
Upstream’s local client is a testing/development backend. Its README directs ordinary use through huggingface_hub. Apache-2.0 permits reuse but does not establish an archival compatibility/support promise. The helper requires the exact tested upstream revision and unknown formats fail; upgrading must not silently reinterpret stored data.
Restart tests passed. Interruption/export qualification passed selected process interruption/retry and stopped-writer ZIP export/import, but failed corruption detection: the default upstream local download returned success with wrong bytes. Unfinished reads also panicked. Those failures remain recorded. The new core independently checks reconstructed length/BLAKE3 in private staging before using the existing guarded destination installer.
A cooperative claim serializes one project’s store operations, including reads which can mutate upstream caches. Finalized verified content precedes immutable snapshot references. No persistent full-file copy is kept, but ingest/restore needs temporary disk space. Sparse database allocation can grow on export/import. A stale claim fails closed; no automatic stale-lock removal or migration occurs.
Snapshots reuse the existing complete file inventory and pure directory identities. A backend-specific binding maps whole-file digests to upstream reconstruction addresses. File digests, directory roots, version metadata and Xet IDs stay distinct. Legacy CAS IDs/readers are untouched.
The dedicated remote integration gate checks exact recovery and complete destination preservation; see the draft PR’s exact-head results. These checks do not establish long-term archival support. Unix runtime only until equivalent hard-link validation is implemented on Windows. No power-loss, concurrent hot-copy, arbitrary interruption-point or production-readiness guarantee follows. Reusing upstream chunk/hash/codec primitives with a proj-owned durable backend is another route, but requires real persistence/index/recovery engineering.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
text:
Save a local copy
Use the matching CLI and helper; no automatic helper installation occurs. The separately built pinned helper must already be on PATH as proj-xet-engine. No build/init/query automatically installs it or logs into Hugging Face. Current runtime support is Unix; Windows proj still works with ordinary backends.
For a project that only archives existing data, an explicit empty script list avoids rerunning an analysis:
directories:
  raw-data:
    path: raw-data
  cache:
    path: cache
    safe: true
remotes:
  local:
    shared-content:
      path: ../experimental-store
      structure: xet
      content: [raw-data]
build:
  scripts: []
  git: false
  dest:
    shared-content: {}
A production build stores selected folders; preview does not upload, require the helper or update backend caches. Queries never activate writes. Removing the remote from build.dest stops uploads while preserving explicit recovery lookup. Optional build.dest content narrows the remote’s eligible labels.
After finalization/independent byte verification, the build saves a complete store snapshot and small project reference under .proj/remotes. The reference’s snapshot field supplies the exact ID:
proj remote verify --title shared-content --snapshot SNAPSHOT_ID
proj remote restore --title shared-content --snapshot SNAPSHOT_ID --label raw-data --clear
Restore uses the label’s configured final directory. Without –clear, extra destination files survive; with it, membership matches the snapshot. Both paths verify private reconstructed bytes before replacement. Verify/restore take the store claim and can update backend caches; they are not byte-for-byte read-only store operations. They leave project VERSION unchanged and need no old project CSV.
Initial configured support is remote full metadata (manifest auto/remote), tree identities and JSON binding. Project/both, flat/CSV/dictionary overrides fail preflight rather than being ignored. Root manifest.csv and old ordinary/CAS formats remain unchanged. Broader format parity is not implemented. GitHub transfer uses this same engine through the complete-store transport described below.
Experimental Xet preview does not copy/restore mutable engine stores under the project-only claim. It never opens the engine, even with an existing busy store. Arbitrary script/hook store edits are outside that preview guarantee. Every production target’s types/format are checked before hooks, independently of one-time helper discovery. The configured integration gate covers multiple targets and busy-store handling.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
section: How the complete store is transferred
text:
How the complete store is transferred
The transport prepares the same local store for complete ZIP transfer. It takes the cooperative store claim while copying stopped-writer persistent data, excludes client caches and writer claims, and validates every committed version using the pinned helper. A separate export manifest records exact file paths, byte lengths and BLAKE3 digests. Unknown store files fail rather than disappearing silently. This is a full-history copy, including orphan packs; it does not reclaim space.
Import first checks the trusted ZIP digest and byte length, then bounded safe extraction, exact file membership, and independent reconstruction of every committed snapshot in a fresh private tree. It never replaces an existing store. Keep the ZIP digest in trusted project/reference metadata; an internal checksum alone does not authenticate an archive.
Configured GitHub publication uses this same transport. Engine and mocked-transport tests passed; final real GitHub evidence is recorded separately. Sparse databases can consume more temporary disk space than their allocated size in the original store. No live-copy or system power-loss guarantee is claimed.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
text:
GitHub transfer and failed uploads
One long-running storage release can hold complete ZIPs of the same local store. The source library uploads a uniquely named ZIP without deleting the previous one, downloads it again, and checks both transport bytes and every stored version before returning a reference. The project must save that reference only after success. A failed or interrupted upload can leave an unreferenced ZIP; the previous reference and export remain available.
Recovery starts from a trusted explicit project reference. The downloaded ZIP opens as a fresh private local store, so adding a version uses exactly the same engine as local storage. The updated complete store is then exported again. GitHub does not run a Xet service, and this initial design transfers the entire ZIP rather than only changed pieces.
There is no automatic latest-export lookup, shared remote writer coordination or cleanup policy. Local engine operations retain their cooperative writer claim. Independent writers can leave separate immutable exports; callers must not silently choose one or claim a merged history. Configured builds use the Git-tracked locators described below.
Complete exports accumulate until an explicit future retention policy is chosen. No automatic deletion is performed. GitHub’s per-asset limit is below 2 GiB; this client rejects larger exports before upload. Temporary expanded database copies can be much larger than the compressed ZIP. Failure tests use a loopback mock REST service. A separate real GitHub round-trip passed with public synthetic bytes; no user datasets were used.

title: Experimental shared-content storage
text:
Keep the store on GitHub
The same local engine and structure selector apply:
directories:
  raw-data:
    path: raw-data
  cache:
    path: cache
    safe: true
  output:
    path: output
remotes:
  github:
    project-data-store:
      structure: xet
      content: [raw-data]
build:
  scripts: []
  git: false
  dest:
    project-data-store: {}
The remote name selects one long-running storage release. The repository comes from the project’s Git origin. Existing GitHub authentication is used; no account, token, engine or R package is installed automatically. Keep credentials out of YAML. The optional pinned engine is required for production only. Preview and queries do not open the engine or contact the release.
Each upload is downloaded and fully checked before writing project metadata under .proj/remotes//xet-github/v1/. The file current.json selects the trusted store for the next build; immutable snapshots//.json locators retain each earlier snapshot’s exact ZIP. Each binds repository, API origin, tag, ZIP name/digest/length, backend/upstream and included snapshot IDs. Keep these files in project Git history. Config relocation must not silently reinterpret old locators; explicit migration is required.
Recover the exact snapshot ID from the project’s locator, then:
proj remote restore --provider github --title project-data-store \
  --snapshot SNAPSHOT_ID --label raw-data --clear \
  --max-bytes 1073741824 --max-expanded-bytes 4294967296

proj remote verify --title project-data-store --snapshot SNAPSHOT_ID \
  --max-bytes 1073741824 --max-expanded-bytes 4294967296
A fresh checkout needs its trusted locators, config, existing authentication and pinned engine. It needs no previous local store, caches, root CSV or current upload selection. If locators are lost, recover them from project Git history instead of guessing by hash or upload time. Full manifests remain in exports; automatic remote-only locator recovery is not implemented.
Production caps ZIPs below 2 GiB and expanded stores at 8 GiB; explicit recovery requires caller-selected budgets. Bounds are not disk reservations. Temporary copies can need much more space than the original sparse database. Every update transfers the complete ZIP; retaining old ZIPs also repeats history on GitHub. Previous exports and failed/orphan uploads remain: there is no automatic retention cleanup, and GitHub asset quotas still apply.
One project uses each store. Project writer exclusion and immutable exports protect local operations and old bytes, but there is no distributed linear-head protocol. Concurrent checkouts can create separate exports and conflicting Git locators; there is no automatic multi-machine history merge.
Xet still repeats a complete readable inventory and file-address binding for each version. Shared directory identities and engine chunk deduplication do not imply version-level inventory deduplication.

title: Build execution flow
text:
This describes the current Rust implementation, not a complete correctness or reproducibility guarantee. The behavior contract records approved semantics and the compatibility log records evidence and gaps.


Capture the project root, resolve a private per-run environment without changing the parent process, require active root configuration, and merge base/profile/local settings. Validate fields, explicit directory paths, targets, hooks and destructive destinations. Explicit empty scripts select no analysis. Otherwise explicit globs or shallow root discovery select inputs; project rendering may use its own input discovery. Explicit Python-only selection does not activate an unused Quarto/Bookdown project marker.
Read VERSION with DESCRIPTION/default fallbacks. Check selected interpreters and configured Git restrictions before controlled project writes. Existing preflight can still invoke Git/network checks or R package remediation; these are known limitations, not a clean-environment guarantee.



Before authoritative writes, capture exact bytes, permissions and presence/absence for the managed set documented in the compatibility log. This includes VERSION, ignore/configuration files, existing root regular files, selected in-project inputs, declared output/docs trees and planned individual rendering artifacts. External declared output/docs directories are allowed. Linked managed trees are rejected. Backups stream into private OS temporary storage outside disposable project cache. Backup creation failure prevents authoritative project writes.
One local error/panic boundary covers ignore synchronization, requested pre-cleanup, pre/both hooks, script/document execution, renderer configuration, promotion and post/both hooks. Required output promotion errors propagate. Renderer configuration is restored exactly, retaining comments and originally absent keys. Candidate version changes stay in memory; VERSION is written only after those stages succeed. No pre-build Git commit is created.
On local failure, restore the captured managed set, including originally absent files/directories. Attempt all restorations; retain recovery backups and report both the primary and restoration errors when recovery fails. This does not undo arbitrary script effects outside the captured set or provide a filesystem sandbox, power-loss atomicity or protection against concurrent filesystem replacement.



Storage export and Git publication start after successful local completion. Export actual declared content before requested clear_output: post cleanup. Create one configured final Git commit, then push when enabled. A publication or later cleanup failure reports that local analysis succeeded and retains its release/version; external publication is not rolled back.
Git upstream/authentication policy, stable attempt/release records and an analysis-free publication retry command remain unfinished. Push uses the captured current-branch upstream; custom push-only routing remains unsupported and fails before authoritative writes. Native authentication is the default.



Previews skip production version changes, cleanup, commits and exports. They run selected hooks/analysis and restore captured managed state after success and failure, while cache output remains. Scripts still choose preview output locations; this is not automatic output redirection or an OS sandbox. Script/hook subprocesses start with the captured invocation cwd by default. Only an explicit project execution mode passes Quarto an execution-directory override; individual R Markdown receives a non-null knit_root_dir only in project mode. Direct R/IDE parity remains unfinished and is not established by these CLI controls. The existing R package remains untouched.
Native execution policy (supersedes earlier unconditional root-cwd wording): build and build-dev default to --execution-dir native. Plain scripts/hooks inherit the invocation cwd, not each source file’s parent; R source() normally inherits its caller cwd. Individual Rmd rendering leaves knit_root_dir unset and Quarto receives no execution-dir override, preserving native document/project settings. --execution-dir project explicitly requests captured-root execution for scripts/hooks, Quarto and individual Rmd. Project render drivers run from the selected project root to select the project, independently of chunk cwd. Project-wide Bookdown root override is currently rejected early because its render_site entrypoint does not expose the individual knit-root argument. Captured project/profile/version and logical path identity do not change with execution cwd. No existing R helper bridge or literal Markdown resource rewriting is implied.

title: What works
text:
v0.4.0-preview.5 provides checked Linux x86-64 (glibc 2.35+) and Windows x86-64 binaries. No Rust compilation is needed. Install that explicit version; GitHub’s stable Latest remains the older v0.3.0.
This development prerelease includes local builds, inspectable build records, readable backup histories and verified recovery of saved local folders. The table summarizes supported Rust CLI behavior; it does not establish R/IDE parity. See the detailed status and delivery evidence for exact verification and limits. Newer changes on main need their own evidence.







Capability
What it means for you




Choose the project
--project PATH selects the folder for a command. Child queries retain that root.


Preview an analysis
build-dev runs your selected steps without CLI version changes, output promotion or archive export.


Read without changing files
Configuration validation and path queries do not create target folders or edit ignore files.


Detect command failures
Errors produce a nonzero exit status, so an automated run can stop.


Run without questions
--non-interactive disables CLI prompts and automatic package installation, and closes runner input.


Select no analysis
An explicit scripts: [] runs no analysis scripts. Hooks may still run; production can export existing outputs.


Run scripts and render documents
The build engine supports Python, R, Quarto and R Markdown/Bookdown targets, with the corresponding tools installed.


Keep a local output archive
Production builds can export configured outputs to local content-addressed storage, which avoids storing identical content repeatedly.





The CLI skips its own release operations during a preview, including cleanup of released outputs and prior caches. This is not a filesystem sandbox. Scripts, hooks and renderers can still change files. Generated-output path queries default to the selected versioned cache. Use those paths from your scripts, as in the tutorial; arbitrary writes are still outside that rule.
Document renderers have their own working folders and output rules. Mixed-language scheduling is not a promise that every target runs in the exact order written in configuration. See the build reference for the current implementation and the behavior contract for limits.

title: What works
section: Known limits of the published preview
text:
Known limits of the published preview

A preview is not a filesystem sandbox. Scripts and hooks control their writes; automatic redirection of every renderer’s output is not provided.
Matching results and paths across CLI runs, RStudio and GUI rendering has not been proved.
Complete compatibility with every projr workflow has not been established.
Mixed script and document targets do not have a complete sequential-order guarantee.
This preview supplies only Linux and Windows x86-64 binaries; macOS and ARM delivery are unavailable.
Production recovery is bounded. It does not undo arbitrary script writes or partial external publication effects.

The existing projr R package is unchanged. The new source package projcli is available in this repository: see its installation and quick start and function reference. It is not on CRAN; preview.5 includes the supported M4 CLI subset and optional R maintenance. Python/Julia frontends and complete R/IDE parity remain separate work.

title: What works
text:
Added in preview.5
Use the separate R package for supported build, path and configuration functions. Optional production actions can generate documentation, render README.Rmd and snapshot renv dependencies; they default off.
Complete CAS stores on GitHub share identical files inside one store. Experimental Xet shares pieces of files locally and uses the same local engine through GitHub ZIPs. Both GitHub options transfer the whole store, keep old immutable exports, and need trusted project references for restore. Xet’s helper is separate and qualified on Linux/WSL; native Windows Xet is unsupported.
The real synthetic round-trip uploaded two versions per structure and restored both into fresh projects. This is bounded test evidence, not whole-projr parity or a dataset savings promise.

title: What works
text:
Planned work
M2 build records and the agreed M3 local recovery scope are included. Full environment reproduction, automatic snapshot discovery and analysis-free publication retry remain separate work. General command/argv steps and stronger execution policies remain follow-ups; they are not silently interpreted from missing script paths.
For the detailed evidence, scope and decisions, see the behavior contract and compatibility log.

title: What works
text:
Included in preview.2
The released CLI keeps a captured project context, defaults generated-output queries to a safe versioned cache, and uses native working folders unless you choose the project-folder override. It supports explicit R-package data management, none/pre/post output cleanup, success-only output promotion and local archives. Supported HTML defaults to embedded resources only when no effective embedding option was supplied; explicit and inherited false remain respected.
Real acceptance covers configured/no-init and fresh directory initialization, ordered Python/R/report steps, a computed CSV and embedded report, structured failures and verified final/archive bytes without Git credentials. See the acceptance and delivery evidence.
Bookdown site embedding is unchanged. Existing R helpers and R/IDE parity, linked HTML portability, complete provenance and publication retry remain outside this claim. The behavior contract remains the detailed source of scope.
Preview.3 includes projr-compatible production CSV inventories, independent of CAS.

title: What works
text:
Remote work in preview.3
Preview.3 can upload selected outputs to ordinary local folders or GitHub Releases, keep versioned snapshots and restore files. It supports comparison by files or recorded history, with explicit controls for what gets uploaded.
A small synthetic project has completed a real GitHub upload, replacement and restore sequence, including reuse of an unchanged archive and preservation of older snapshots. See the remote verification and command reference for the tested scope and limits.
These ordinary remote additions were introduced in preview.3 and remain in preview.4. The separate test prerelease holds sample data, not an installer. Complete projr compatibility remains unproved. Preview.4 adds the named locations and file histories below.

title: What works
section: Choose where a build saves its results
text:
Choose where a build saves its results
In preview.4, name each available storage destination once under remotes, then select where this build sends its results with build.dest. A named location remains available for restoring earlier data after you stop uploading to it. The configuration reference has copyable examples and explains how to select only particular folders.
For local content-addressed storage (CAS), identical file bytes are stored once and folders receive fingerprints based on their names and contents. The new tree writer can keep the complete folder listing in the storage location, in your project, or in both. It always keeps a small project record identifying the saved folders. That small record alone cannot restore files if the storage content or required full listings are lost.
These additions are included in preview.4. Automatic version selection for CAS restore remains deferred; local CAS CSV/JSON history is described below. Explicit named-ID tree recovery is described below. Ordinary local and GitHub Release upload/restore behavior remains available as described in the remote guide.

title: What works
section: Check and recover a saved folder
text:
Check and recover a saved folder
In preview.4, you can check the exact file bytes in a local tree snapshot, then restore a selected folder. Choose its configured storage name and snapshot ID explicitly; this first command slice does not find a version for you. The remote reference shows both commands.
Restoring an older folder still works after you stop uploading that folder. A complete snapshot saved remotely can recover files into a fresh configured project. The command leaves your project version and stored snapshot unchanged. It checks the data before replacing files; choose –clear only when you want to remove destination-only files as well. This is included in preview.4.
Existing flat CAS snapshots can also be checked and restored by exact ID without converting them. See the remote reference. Their older file lists do not record empty folders, so those cannot be restored from that format. Local CAS CSV/JSON history is described below; ordinary/GitHub flat publication is also implemented below; Ordinary local and GitHub tree metadata are described below.

title: What works
section: Keep a readable history of saved files
text:
Keep a readable history of saved files
In preview.4, a local store can keep a CSV history you can filter in Excel, or a JSON history you can open as text. When a folder has not changed, a later version points directly to its earlier complete listing. Changed versions still list every current file. The configuration example shows how to choose the format and where to keep the full history.
You can optionally shorten repeated hashes using a file dictionary. That adds indirection, so it is off by default. File-byte storage already avoids duplicate content independently of these choices. The existing project manifest.csv remains unchanged. These additions are included in preview.4.

title: What works
section: See which files reached a local backup
text:
See which files reached a local backup
In preview.4, local folder backups can keep readable CSV or JSON lists for each build. The list describes files actually stored, including older files your upload settings deliberately keep. An unchanged folder points to its earlier complete listing. CSV stays suitable for filtering in Excel: a reference row tells you which earlier version to filter.
For archived backups, the record also tells you which physical version folder contains the bytes. Keeping the latest folder replaces its older contents; a historical list does not recreate bytes that have since been overwritten. See the configuration example. This addition is included in preview.4.

title: What works
section: Keep a readable file history with GitHub backups
text:
Keep a readable file history with GitHub backups
In preview.4, GitHub backups can also keep CSV or JSON file lists. Choose which folders to upload, save a complete listing in the project, on GitHub, or both, and retain a small project record pointing to the saved files. An unchanged folder can point to an earlier complete listing. Optional formats can reduce repeated file information while retaining every filename.
The list describes the ZIP actually prepared for upload. If an archived folder is reused, its record names that older ZIP. A failed upload keeps the local release and reports that some files may already have been sent. The tool avoids replacing a history bundle that another writer changed while the build ran. See the copyable example and limits. This addition is included in preview.4. HTTP transport tests use synthetic local servers; they are not a new live GitHub round-trip claim.

title: What works
section: Keep folder fingerprints with local backups
text:
Keep folder fingerprints with local backups
Preview.4 can give each saved folder a code based on its filenames and contents. Unchanged subfolders keep the same codes across builds. Backups retain their normal versioned folders, and a readable JSON history still shows the complete file lists or points to the earlier unchanged listing.
Choose tree style in this local-backup example. The small project record keeps the folder code even when complete metadata stays with the backup. This addition is included in preview.4.

title: What works
section: Keep folder fingerprints with GitHub backups
text:
Keep folder fingerprints with GitHub backups
GitHub backups normally keep a flat file list. You can also save fingerprints for each folder and its children, while keeping the same downloadable data ZIPs. Set manifest-style: tree on that remote; the configuration reference gives a complete example and explains where the listings are saved.
The saved file list describes what actually reached the ZIP, including retained older files when your upload settings request them. Identical folder contents have the same fingerprint across versions. A small project record identifies the saved root even when full listings live on GitHub. Earlier flat records remain readable when you change this setting. This feature is included in preview.4.

title: Preview release delivery
text:
The reviewed pipeline prepares a draft prerelease for an existing vX.Y.Z-preview.N tag whose version exactly matches Cargo.toml. It does not bump versions, push commits, publish an APT repository, sign credentials or publish the draft automatically. No new release is implied by this documentation.
Remote locked tests/builds produce Linux x86-64 and Windows x86-64 binaries. Linux uses Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35 or newer); the initial user-local WSL installation target is Ubuntu 24.04 x86-64. macOS/ARM delivery is not verified or supplied by this pipeline. Each asset is named proj_<version>_<os>_<arch>[.exe], with matching version.txt and checksums.txt. Exact-tag help/version/protocol smokes and actual installer tests must pass before assets enter the draft. Checksums detect corruption and mismatches; they are not independent signatures or reproducible-build attestations.
Installers default to MiguelRodo/projcli, require version metadata and exactly one matching SHA256 entry, and verify downloaded bytes before replacement. They stage on the installation filesystem and need only an existing user-writable directory. PROJ_RELEASE_VERSION pins a release (with optional v); preview releases should always be pinned because GitHub’s latest URL normally selects stable releases. PROJ_INSTALL_DIR selects an existing absolute user directory without changing PATH or system settings. Existing older releases lacking the new metadata fail closed instead of installing an unverified fallback binary.
Before publication: reconcile reviewed supported behavior and limits, update the Cargo/Cargo.lock preview version in a reviewed change, verify required checks, then create the exact reviewed tag. Inspect the resulting draft assets/version/ checksums and retain disposable-project warnings. Publish only after those checks. For WSL, download the pinned binary/manifest, verify SHA256, preserve any existing user-local binary, install into the chosen user-local directory and smoke help, version, capabilities and a disposable configured preview. No local compilation, sudo, persistent authentication change or R package modification is needed.
Known limits include bounded captured-state recovery, arbitrary external script effects, incomplete direct R/IDE parity, analysis-free publication retry and broader environment reproduction. Preview.4 includes the agreed M2/M3 scope described below.

title: projcli 0.4.0-preview.5
text:
This preview adds experimental Xet storage and complete CAS/Xet store transfer through GitHub Releases, plus the R interface and optional R build tasks introduced since preview.4. Release assets include source-commit.txt and checksums.txt; use those files to identify the exact reviewed source and platform download.



From R, preview/build projects, query configuration and resolve file paths using the separate thin projcli package. See the website’s R package guide and function reference. It is available from source, not CRAN; the standalone command is installed separately. The original SATVILab/projr package is unchanged.
Optional build.r actions generate documentation, render README.Rmd and snapshot renv dependencies. Each is off by default. Snapshot ordering follows projr. Explicit init readme –rmd and init renv commands do not replace existing state.
Optional local structure: xet shares chunks within files using a separately built exact-pinned helper. Upstream’s local backend is experimental. The core verifies independent whole-file BLAKE3 and length in private staging before installing restored files; successful upstream return values alone are insufficient.
GitHub structure: xet uses the same local engine through complete-store ZIPs. GitHub structure: cas transports the existing whole-file store and preserves tree, flat CSV/JSON/dictionary and legacy snapshots. Ordinary latest/archive uploads and local file CAS remain compatible.
Each configured store uses one long-running storage release. A new immutable, checksum-named ZIP is uploaded, downloaded and validated before its trusted project reference can change. Prior good assets are retained. Failed or uncertain operations can leave an unreferenced ZIP; they do not delete the old store.
The website introduces the R package prominently and provides storage guides. Changed-source CI checks Rustfmt/Clippy and Air/lintr without contributor writes.




Xet runtime is currently Linux/Unix only, needs the separately pinned optional helper, and is not a production archival guarantee. No Hugging Face account or service is required for this local engine. File/chunk sharing depends on actual bytes; already-compressed files may share little. Xet snapshot inventories remain complete per-version documents; chunk sharing is not metadata delta encoding.
GitHub transfers complete ZIPs, not incremental chunks. Initial configured support requires full metadata in the remote store (manifest: auto or remote); unsupported placement/style options fail before hooks. GitHub CAS requires an explicit manifest-style: tree or flat. Both use project Git metadata to identify the trusted ZIP; missing project authority is an error, not permission to guess a latest export. Back up that metadata. Each store belongs to one project.
Exports require stopped/cooperative writers; no hot-copy, power-loss, distributed locking, automatic migration, retention cleanup or garbage collection guarantee. Outer hashes, strict ZIP membership/path/size checks and deep reconstruction verification precede guarded installation. Temporary disk requirements can exceed the ZIP size, and sparse databases can expand. Arbitrary scripts remain able to modify files; this is not a sandbox.
The unrelated pending initialization/scripts PRs are not part of this release. No new general citation helpers, DESCRIPTION synchronization or glob/routing features are claimed here. End-hook mutation enforcement remains deferred.



Final exact-head/main, platform, real synthetic GitHub round-trip, independently verified artifacts, release checksum and installed-path results must be attached to the delivery checkpoint before this candidate is described as published. Synthetic tests do not establish all real workload savings or whole projr parity.

title: Configuration _proj.yml
text:
Preview.4 includes the named remote definitions, file-history formats and explicit local snapshot recovery documented below. Historical slice notes retain their original verification scope. See verified delivery.
The _proj.yml file dictates the structural map of your project. It configures the foundational paths and mapping logic used by the CLI.


Custom directory labels are strictly validated against a set of foundational prefixes: - cache - raw - output - docs
These prefixes are case-insensitive. Any label defined in the configuration must begin with one of these approved identifiers.



Ordinary declared directories need a nonempty path. The fixed R-package role output-r-data: {} is the exception: its final destination is project/data. Runtime does not insert other missing cache/raw/output/docs mappings or synthesize subpaths for undeclared labels. Canonical data/data-* labels are rejected; see the R-package data section for the legacy per-layer data alias. For example, declaring raw-data: {path: _raw_data} makes raw-data available; it does not create an undeclared raw or raw-data-extra resource. ASCII case is ignored and case-only duplicate labels are rejected.
proj --project . --non-interactive init directories creates a missing _proj.yml once with explicit raw-data: _raw_data, cache: _tmp, and output: _output paths. It preserves existing base/profile files, creates only declared resource directories, and does not invoke Git/GitHub or add an R code directory. The preset omits build.scripts, preserving shallow discovery; it never serializes an accidental empty analysis list. To render documents, declare a docs mapping too.
Production state and project-render staging require a declared cache directory. Framework version/staging children are derived inside that declared cache; this is distinct from inventing undeclared resource labels. Storage content labels must be declared and relative storage paths use the captured project root.



Each cache-class directory may include boolean safe. One explicit safe: true selects that cache; otherwise an eligible exact cache label wins, then the first eligible cache in merged declaration order. safe: false excludes a candidate. Profile/local overrides retain existing declaration positions. For example:
directories:
  cache:
    path: _tmp
  cache-analysis:
    path: _analysis_cache
    safe: true
This selects _analysis_cache for explicit safe logical output lookup. Multiple true selections, non-boolean values (including null), selection flags on non-cache roles, and all declared cache candidates excluded are validation errors. Each layer’s explicit values are checked before merging; null cannot inherit a previous boolean. Cache-free queries and operations that do not consume a cache remain valid. The chosen safe cache is frozen in child run context. Cleanup, safe lookup and renderer staging consume that same selected mapping; no literal cache label is required when another eligible cache is selected.



The system performs strict validation on _proj.yml: - If a defined directory label uses an unsupported prefix layout, a validation error string will be returned and execution will fail. - All references must resolve correctly; otherwise, the CLI will output an error detailing the structurally invalid labels or malformed content.



The _proj.yml file supports a top-level config block for project-wide settings:

config.git.engine: The Git execution engine to use. Can be auto (default) or system. This determines how the CLI interfaces with Git capabilities natively.
config.git.use_proj_cred_helper: Defaults to false: use existing native Git authentication. Explicit true permits an existing single-line GITHUB_PAT, GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN for standard HTTPS github.com remotes through a temporary host-scoped helper. There is no automatic token discovery or GitHub CLI call during builds. Tokens are environment data, never argv or shell source; persistent auth settings are unchanged.




The _proj.yml file supports a top-level parameters block for arbitrary nested parameter evaluation. This allows you to define custom metadata and deeply queried values throughout your execution environment.
The configuration engine also supports several aliases for this block: parameter, params, and param. However, multiple alias conflicts within the same configuration file are structurally rejected during validation to prevent mapping confusion.



The _proj.yml file supports a top-level remotes block, which currently supports a local mapping of standalone storage vaults.

local: A mapping where keys represent remote titles and values configure the vault:

path: The physical absolute or relative path to the remote storage directory.
structure: Specifies the storage structure algorithm. Must be cas (Content-Addressable Storage).
content: An array of string tags (matching foundational prefixes or defined directories) specifying which project output directories to sync into the remote upon build completion.
inspect: manifest validates JSON, logical paths/digests and manifest filename/content identity; file additionally hashes every referenced object and compares actual bytes. Manifest-only inspection does not verify object bytes.





The _proj.yml file can also contain a build block to configure the behavior of the proj build and proj build-dev execution engine. The build block supports the following sub-keys:

dest: An optional list of remote target strings. These targets must be mapped to explicit configurations within the remotes.local block. During post-build execution, resolved content directories matching these tags are piped to the CAS engine for deduplicated storage synchronization.
scripts: An optional list of explicit script paths or glob patterns to execute during the build pipeline.

Globbing patterns are supported.
Prefix a pattern with ! to exclude matching files from execution.
Current source rejects malformed inclusion or exclusion syntax before execution, including hook patterns. The exclusion correction is included in preview.3; see the build reference.
When provided, this selects scripts instead of automatic discovery. Document targets may be grouped for rendering, so mixed script and document targets are not guaranteed to run in the exact listed order.

hooks: An optional map of lifecycle hook scripts to execute.

pre: Scripts executed before the actual build phase.
post: Scripts executed after analysis/promotion, before VERSION and publication.
both: Scripts executed during both pre and post phases.

profile: An optional environment profile identifier. When set, the system injects the PROJR_PROFILE environment variable into the isolated subprocess for all executed scripts and project rendering commands. This can be overridden at runtime via the --profile CLI flag.
git: An optional Git integration configuration. This can be a boolean toggle or an object mapping out detailed toggles:

commit: Defaults to false, including inside an existing Git repository. Explicit true requires initially clean Git state and commits once after successful local build; an unchanged staged index is a successful no-op.
push: Defaults to false. Explicit true publishes HEAD to the current branch’s configured upstream remote/reference. Missing upstream or custom push-only routing fails before build writes; origin/main is never invented.

restrictions: Configuration block to enforce Git checks specifically during production builds:

only_branches: A list of allowed branch names. Production builds will abort if the current branch is not in this list.
not_branches: A list of restricted branch names. Production builds will abort if the current branch is in this list.
not_behind: Omitted/false performs no fetch. Explicit true fetches the current configured upstream and compares its state. If enabled, production builds will verify that the local branch has an upstream tracking remote and is not behind it, aborting if the local branch needs to pull upstream changes.

clear_output: An optional string controlling workspace clearing routines for output directories. Can be set to "pre", "post", or "never". If omitted, defaults to evaluating the PROJR_CLEAR_OUTPUT environment variable.




You can define a dev block to completely override specific configurations during development builds (proj build-dev).

scripts: A list of script paths or globs. During development builds, this array entirely overrides build.scripts. An explicitly empty array ([]) selects no analysis scripts. An absent dev.scripts inherits build.scripts. Hooks can still run.
hooks: A mapping identical to build.hooks. When specified, these completely replace build.hooks during a development build.
old_dev_remove: Retained configuration field. The current preview protections skip CLI cleanup of prior caches during development builds, even when this is true. Scripts and hooks still control their own writes.





PROJR_AUTO_INSTALL: During the proj build pre-flight checks, if required R packages (like bookdown or rmarkdown) are missing, this environment variable controls remediation. If set to true, packages are automatically installed. If absent or set to false, the tool defaults to an interactive terminal prompt (if available) or fails hard.




build declares actions; settings controls how they run. Parameters are analysis inputs, not execution controls. This is an intentional extension beyond projr.
settings:
  output-clear-stage: none
  execution-directory: native
  path-representation: auto
Use none to preserve other existing final files, pre to clear immediately before analysis, or post to clear immediately after successful analysis and before output promotion/finalization. Preview never clears released outputs. Pre-hooks run before pre-clear; end hooks run after finalization immediately before the next-dev bump. The command’s explicit –output-clear-stage overrides merged settings; those override legacy build.clear_output, then PROJR_CLEAR_OUTPUT, then the new none default. Legacy never is accepted in the legacy field/environment. The canonical settings key accepts only none/pre/post, with invalid values/null rejected before merge or mutation. execution-directory accepts native/project; explicit --execution-dir wins over merged settings, then native is the fallback. Native scripts inherit launch cwd; native document execution remains renderer-defined. path-representation accepts auto/absolute/relative; explicit path-query --format wins over merged settings, then auto is the fallback. Auto is caller-relative ordinarily and absolute in a known managed renderer. Both settings reject null, booleans and unknown values in each active file before merging. Managed child queries retain the captured representation policy even if scripts change configuration, profiles or cwd. Safe is the default path target; final must be explicitly requested. Docs output handling and the R-data built-in remain separately modeled features.



The built-in output-r-data lookup has fixed final destination project/data, even without YAML. Querying never activates build management or creates directories. Safe lookup needs the selected declared cache and active version.
To opt into ordinary output clearing and success-only promotion:
directories:
  cache:
    path: _tmp
  output-r-data:
    ignore: []
An empty output-r-data mapping also activates the role, with ordinary default ignore rules. Explicit ignore: [] includes package data in Git and R builds. The path may be omitted; if present it must resolve to project/data. Redirection is forbidden. settings.output-clear-stage applies normally: pre/post clears old package data; the default none preserves other final files. Preview never promotes final data.
Legacy _projr.yml and active _projr-*.yml layers accept data as an alias and normalize it before merging, including legacy remote content labels. Defining both aliases in one layer is an error. Canonical _proj.yml requires output-r-data. Generic data-* labels are unsupported; use raw-* inputs or ordinary output-* mappings.



CAS ingestion records the current recursive file paths and content hashes for the explicitly selected directory. The transition fixture compares exact inventories and stored bytes after a same-size/same-modified-time edit, an addition, a rename and a deletion. Earlier snapshots remain inspectable across those later ingestions. A renamed file appears under its new path in the current snapshot; this does not create a rename-event format.
This verifies existing archive machinery only. It does not automatically record all build inputs, code, configuration or dependencies, select a future build record format, or decide content-only identity and retention policy. Complete M2 provenance remains unfinished.



Current source adds directory boolean hash. It defaults to true for declared raw/output/docs labels and false for cache labels. Set hash: false to omit a directory, or hash: true to include a cache. Each active layer must use a boolean; null, numbers and strings fail validation before hooks.
directories:
  raw-data: {path: inputs}
  cache: {path: _tmp, hash: false}
  output: {path: results}
A successful output-enabled production build writes root manifest.csv, without requiring Git or a remote. Preview and build.output_run: false leave that CSV alone. See the inventory notes. This CSV capture is included in preview.3. See the compatibility log and PR175 for verification evidence.



The current source’s explicit remote restore command reads the existing projr directories.LABEL.source and build.local/build.github definitions. See the remote command reference for lookup precedence, limits and safety. This does not enable automatic ordinary uploads in build; normal build validation still rejects unsupported publication fields. The future top-level registry proposal remains separate. _proj.yml and legacy _projr.yml discovery/conflict rules remain unchanged.
Configured restore uses the shared profile selection order: explicit profile, PROJR_PROFILE, QUARTO_PROFILE, then build.profile, with earlier profiles winning and local overrides last. Machine failures preserve installation/recovery details on stderr, including retained backup paths; stdout stays a structured failure. Legacy data CSV rows and remote data namespaces are read without rewriting history; ambiguous canonical/legacy namespaces fail before installation. One optional VERSION trust marker is accepted; it is not a byte-verification claim.
Review precision: VERSION.zip requires exactly the canonical VERSION member spelling, including on case-insensitive filesystems. Metadata transfer staging also closes explicitly and reports cleanup failure paths.



build.local.TITLE accepts selected latest destinations with explicit send.inspect:file. See the remote command reference for the complete example and tested/pending control matrix. content:false/null disables a destination, true selects declared non-cache roles, and a list retains its explicit label order. Each selected role must have CSV hash capture enabled. The existing if-change/sync-diff defaults remain; omitted inspect does not silently change the projr manifest default to file.
Archive, manifest/none inspection, path-append-label:false, title-level cue and nonempty get/conflict controls are not executable in this bounded slice. Selected unsupported policy fails before hooks. Registry706 remains design-only.
For configured ordinary local latest publication, explicit send.inspect: none selects blind source-file planning and defaults send.strategy to upload-all. Explicit upload-missing/sync-diff then overwrite source filenames while retaining remote extras; sync-purge only purges when the source is nonempty. See the remote control matrix before choosing these combinations. Omitted inspection retains the projr manifest default, using matching recorded history or falling back to physical file comparison.
Configured ordinary build.local publication now follows the archive default when structure is omitted; latest remains explicit. The existing manifest inspection and sync-diff/if-change defaults apply. See archive publication for historical reuse, complete snapshots and unsupported append-label:false.
The first build.github upload subset requires explicit send.inspect: none and upload-all (the none default), with archive as the existing structure default. Other decision combinations and existing current-version data fail explicitly. See the remote CLI page for credentials, metadata bounds and partial failure.



Ordinary local latest/archive and GitHub Release definitions can now live under top-level remotes rather than build. A definition remains available to restore even when the build no longer uploads to it. These use the same executable definition/send fields already accepted by inline ordinary publication.
remotes:
  local:
    historical:
      path: ../historical-store
      structure: archive
      content: [raw-data]
    current:
      path: ../current-store
      structure: latest
      send:
        cue: if-change
        inspect: manifest
build:
  dest:
    current:
      content: [output]
  scripts: []
  git: false
A selected destination’s content list limits that build to declared labels allowed by the remote’s content, if specified. Omit the destination’s content to use all remote-eligible labels; if the remote also omits content, ordinary content:true selection applies (declared non-cache labels, with existing hash requirements). Explicit content:[] selects no labels. build.dest:{} selects no registered uploads. Registry membership alone does not upload or load GitHub credentials.
Normal builds now accept and validate the existing directory source metadata:
directories:
  raw-data:
    path: data
    source:
      local: historical
This does not automatically restore during a build. Use the existing remote restore command with –label, optionally –title/–provider and explicit version/clear choices. Source lookup uses the registry independently of build.dest. Directory-specific references keep priority. Existing legacy preferred sources win first; an explicitly preferred registered source can win over an unpreferred legacy fallback. Otherwise legacy fallback order remains ahead of newly available registry fallback definitions.
Unknown names, duplicate/portable-aliased registered names, invalid/excluded label subsets and conflicting registry/inline definitions fail before hooks or writes. The new mapping selection cannot be mixed with inline build.local/build.github; move those definitions to remotes first. Empty/omitted subsets are distinct from null; explicitly null/malformed mapping entries are rejected. Remote-level content:null retains its existing disabled/no-label meaning and cannot be overridden by a build subset.
Legacy inline ordinary builds and legacy CAS name-list destinations retain their existing path. Purely legacy CAS name lists do not acquire new case-folding rules. The new registry also accepts an ordinary name list for all eligible content, while mapping form is required for per-build label subsets.
Named ordinary local destinations now support flat CSV/JSON history and metadata placement, described below. GitHub flat/tree metadata is also implemented below. Configured CAS tree mapping publication is described below. The existing CAS name-list route retains its legacy flat encoding when using legacy definitions. Previously stored snapshots and the explicit tree APIs remain unchanged.



New local CAS definitions can select recursive tree publication through the named registry. Directory selection is independent of full metadata placement:
remotes:
  local:
    snapshots:
      path: ../snapshot-store
      structure: cas
      manifest: auto
      manifest-style: tree
build:
  dest:
    snapshots:
      content: [raw, output]
Omitted content selects eligible non-cache declared labels. Explicit null, false or an empty list selects none; build subsets cannot enable excluded labels. auto means remote for this CAS writer. remote stores complete tree objects and snapshot metadata beside file objects; project stores that metadata under the project; both requires both copies. File objects always remain in the configured store. A small project reference is retained for every successful publication, including remote placement. That reference is not itself a complete archive.
Raw objects, directory objects and snapshot/reference records use first-two- characters/rest-of-hash fan-out. Identical directory contents share a root across labels and versions. Snapshot version associations are separate immutable records. There is no inferred timestamp or mutable discovery index. Existing blobs are verified before reuse. Required graphs precede full references; the small project reference is written last. Errors after provider entry retain the local release and distribution evidence. both is not a cross-location atomic transaction: partial references/objects may remain and errors say so. Nothing is garbage- collected or rolled back from a published store automatically.
Previously accepted path/structure/content/inspect CAS definitions keep their legacy flat JSON identities and plural .projr/manifests.csv ledger. Name-list selection still works; mapping subsets preserve legacy label spelling. To opt into new trees, remove the legacy inspect field and explicitly select tree if desired. No old manifest is reinterpreted or moved.
The first publication slice added tree storage. Explicit named-ID recovery and local CAS flat CSV/JSON histories are described below. Automatic snapshot lookup remains deferred. Legacy inspect belongs only to the old definition; new manifest-format choices are validated against style. Ordinary local/GitHub flat histories are also implemented below, alongside compatible CSV/VERSION metadata; Ordinary local and GitHub tree metadata are described below.



The explicit CAS restore/verify commands use a named remotes.local definition and saved snapshot ID. They do not run build.dest selection or require the current write style/placement to match the older snapshot. The destination label must still be declared. Existing full remote and project metadata are checked; no root manifest.csv or mutable index is required. Normal directory-source preference remains the ordinary restore selection contract when no snapshot ID is supplied.
Existing flat CAS snapshots can also be checked and restored by exact ID without converting them. See the remote reference. Their older file lists do not record empty folders, so those cannot be restored from that format. Local CAS CSV/JSON history is described below; ordinary/GitHub flat publication is also implemented below; Ordinary local and GitHub tree metadata are described below.



New local CAS remotes can save a readable CSV or JSON history instead of a directory-tree manifest:
remotes:
  local:
    snapshots:
      path: ../snapshot-store
      structure: cas
      manifest-style: flat
      manifest-format: csv
      manifest: remote
build:
  dest:
    snapshots:
      content: [raw, output]
The labels must already be declared. For flat style, csv is the default; json is also available. Both automatically reuse an earlier complete inventory for the same logical folder when later contents are identical, including a reversion to older contents. The later version points directly to that earlier complete version, never a chain. A changed version records all current file memberships, including additions, removals and renamed paths.
CSV is one rectangular table with a header and repeated label/version columns. In Excel, filtering a reference version shows the earlier ref_version to inspect; it does not automatically expand that earlier listing. All earlier complete rows remain in the same history file. Plain CSV/JSON retains literal full file hashes. Optional csv-dedupe-file/json-dedupe-file modes replace repeated hashes with a bundled file dictionary while retaining every file path. These modes are off by default. They are not omitted-file deltas, and no size/speed advantage is promised.
Files are stored once by their BLAKE3 content hash regardless of manifest format. Full history files live under catalogues/v1/manifest.csv or manifest.json; opt-in dictionary files use manifest-dedupe-file.csv/json. Existing root manifest.csv keeps its separate projr-compatible MD5 schema and is unchanged.
auto means remote for CAS. project/remote/both selects full history placement; a small project snapshot binding is always retained. Flat bindings connect the version and selected labels to inventory hashes, independently of serialization or dictionary IDs. They are not directory-tree object IDs. Full immutable refs use flat-snapshots/v1/<first2>/<rest62>.json; small project refs use references/flat-v1/<first2>/<rest62>.json. No unnecessary tree objects are written.
History replacement is atomic per file. Decoded previous label/version contents are never overwritten; divergent histories or conflicting same-version retries fail. Identical per-label retries do not duplicate rows, and missing labels can resume a partial write. Switching format preserves older files/readability and uses the longest compatible decoded history; dictionary IDs do not define it. Codec limits fail explicitly rather than truncating history.
The authoritative history read through replacement/reference publication holds the existing cooperative claim at <store>/.proj/build.lock. Unknown/stale claims fail closed and only an owned claim is removed; there is no automatic process killing or stale-claim cleanup. Raw immutable objects may be copied before that claim. Required history copies precede full snapshot refs, then the small project ref. both is not a cross-location transaction: errors can leave objects or an updated first history copy. Retry can finish the remaining copy.
Explicit verify/restore resolves version references/dictionaries, checks inventory hashes and actual raw bytes, and uses the existing guarded installer. The result reports snapshot_kind: flat-catalogue-v1. Old tree and legacy-flat IDs stay distinct and readable, regardless of the current write style. A small binding alone is not a backup. Empty directories are recorded by this new format, unlike legacy flat.
These manifest-format controls apply to local CAS and the ordinary local/GitHub flat histories described below. Ordinary providers retain compatible CSV/VERSION metadata alongside the new histories. CAS trees default to fixed v1 JSON; explicit manifest-format: json is valid there, while CSV/dictionary choices require flat style. Null/unknown modes fail instead of silently choosing a default.



Development source supports the four flat manifest formats for named local latest/archive destinations:
remotes:
  local:
    backup:
      path: ../backup
      structure: archive
      manifest: both
      manifest-style: flat
      manifest-format: csv
build:
  dest:
    backup:
      content: [raw, output]
Here csv is the default; json, csv-dedupe-file and json-dedupe-file are also supported. Identical complete inventories for the same logical folder reference the earlier complete version. Optional dictionaries retain every path row. The build version identifies the observation; its file hashes describe the actual final destination, including older files retained by upload-missing or upload-all. This is separate from the project’s source CSV.
manifest:auto defaults to both for ordinary local destinations. project stores complete new history only in the project; remote stores it only under the remote’s .projcli-manifests directory; both stores both. Complete catalogue files use the same catalogues/v1 filenames as local CAS. A small project binding is always written last under .proj/remotes and records the physical folder, empty marker and verbatim legacy VERSION entry. The binding alone is not a complete file list.
Unchanged archive data may stay in an older physical version directory; the new build record points there. Latest records describe what was observed, without making older overwritten bytes recoverable. An asterisk in legacy VERSION still means source agreement is untrusted; hashing actual destination bytes does not remove it. Root MD5 manifest.csv, VERSION and CHANGELOG.md remain the existing compatibility metadata regardless of the new manifest placement.
Pure legacy inline build.local definitions keep their old behavior unless an explicit manifest/style/format field opts in. Null or unknown options fail. Ordinary local tree metadata and GitHub flat formatting are described below; GitHub tree metadata is described below. Switching formats retains old files and reads compatible earlier history; conflicting retries or histories fail rather than overwrite recorded inventory.
A cooperative destination claim covers history reads through publication. Required full catalogues precede immutable full bindings and the small project binding. Multiple copies are not a transaction: failure may leave earlier data or metadata installed, and is reported as partial publication.
Changing ordinary local placement reads compatible history from both fixed known locations, but writes complete history only to the newly selected locations. Old unselected files remain intact; changing placement or format cannot silently start a disconnected history.



Development source uses flat CSV by default for named GitHub Release destinations:
remotes:
  github:
    analysis-files:
      structure: archive
      manifest: both
      manifest-format: json
build:
  dest:
    analysis-files:
      content: [raw, output]
The same four flat formats and auto/project/remote/both placements as ordinary local destinations apply. auto means both. The format default remains csv; Tree style is available for ordinary local destinations; GitHub tree style is also described below. Legacy inline build.github without new metadata fields retains its old behavior.
Complete new remote history is a separate projcli-manifests-v1.zip Release asset, containing versioned catalogue files and immutable snapshot bindings. Existing manifest.zip, VERSION.zip and CHANGELOG.zip retain their compatibility purpose. Project full history, when selected, lives under the provider-separated .proj/remotes name; a small project binding is always kept. Names, not upload selection, still determine which registered remotes remain available sources.
Recorded inventories describe exact prepared ZIP payloads or a physically downloaded reused archive. They never describe an empty catalog placeholder. Bindings retain the frozen repository/tag, actual asset filename, empty variant, inventory hash and existing VERSION advertisement separately from the build version. The ZIP writer’s omitted empty child folders are not falsely recorded. Legacy root MD5 manifest.csv and VERSION* meanings remain unchanged.
History is read from the two fixed known locations across format/placement changes. Old files remain readable and are not silently migrated or deleted. Bundles reject unknown members, conflicting/corrupt histories and unsafe paths; compressed and expanded limits are 128 MiB, individual metadata files 16 MiB, and native ZIP member count at most 100,000 including directory entries. Generated bundles must pass the same reader before uploads.
All targets prepare before HTTP writes. Data and legacy metadata precede each new bundle. Replacing a bundle requires its asset identity to match the original observation; a newer asset fails without deleting it. This is optimistic protection, not distributed locking or a remote transaction. All required target HTTP writes and project full metadata writes precede small project references. Later failures preserve local release and honest partial-publication evidence, without automatic rollback or retry. Ordinary restore continues the compatible metadata path.


For configured flat CAS, both fixed known metadata locations are guarded/read regardless of selected write placement. Changing project to remote to both, even while switching CSV/JSON modes, preserves the longest compatible complete history. Only selected full locations are written; old unselected files remain intact. A conflicting known copy fails before hooks rather than silently discarding it. Reads are rechecked under the store writer claim before publication. Existing exact-ID snapshots remain recoverable. This is fixed-location continuity, not automatic snapshot discovery or a migration.




Ordinary local data keeps its latest/archive folder layout while directory metadata can use the same v1 content identities as native CAS:
remotes:
  local:
    backup:
      path: ../backup
      structure: archive
      manifest-style: tree
      manifest: remote
      # Optional for tree style; JSON is the fixed representation.
      manifest-format: json
build:
  dest:
    backup:
      content: [raw, output]
Defaults remain flat for ordinary local/GitHub destinations and tree for modern local CAS. Ordinary local tree metadata uses JSON; CSV/file-dictionary choices require flat style. GitHub tree metadata is also supported as described below. Legacy inline definitions opt in by specifying new metadata fields.
Directory objects live at trees/v1/<first2>/<remaining62>.json inside the selected full metadata location. Each child’s name/type/content hash determines its directory ID; labels, build versions, physical paths and catalogue serialization are excluded. No ordinary data is copied into a CAS objects directory.
The complete JSON catalogue remains a readable companion and immutable-version lookup, with the existing direct references to earlier complete inventories. Tree roots are derived independently and checked against that exact membership. This duplicates some metadata deliberately; neither reduced size nor speed has been established. Old flat bindings remain unchanged; a distinct projcli.ordinary-local-tree-snapshot.v1 binding adds each payload’s tree root, separate from inventory_hash and its physical data location.
Placement chooses full directory-object/history/binding copies. A small project reference still records the root when full metadata is remote. Required directory objects and full histories precede full bindings and the small project reference. Changing style/format preserves old files and compatible history.
Each final private payload is checked before replacing its existing directory, including Tree representability; the complete selected forest is checked again at metadata publication. Bounds include 100,000 inferred records including roots, 64 path components, 4,096 path bytes, 16 MiB cumulative expanded path work and 64 MiB unique directory metadata per forest. Each object retains the existing 16 MiB document bound. Node IDs are checked before following them; links and special files fail. Multi-label/multi-location publication is not a transaction: later failure may leave earlier effects and preserves local release/evidence.
Ordinary restore remains the compatible CSV/VERSION operation. Its file data is still the normal backup folder. The separate exact-ID CAS recovery commands do not reinterpret these ordinary bindings as CAS file-object snapshots.



GitHub Release destinations keep their ordinary data ZIPs and flat default. To opt into directory-based fingerprints, set tree style on the named remote:
remotes:
  github:
    backup:
      structure: archive
      manifest-style: tree
      manifest: remote
      # Optional; tree metadata has a fixed JSON representation.
      manifest-format: json
build:
  dest:
    backup:
      content: [raw, output]
The Release receives projcli-manifests-v1.zip containing the readable JSON history, directory objects at trees/v1/<first2>/<remaining62>.json and immutable snapshot bindings. The project retains a small root reference even with remote placement. Project/both placement additionally saves full selected metadata under the existing provider-separated project location. Auto retains ordinary both behavior. Tree style requires JSON; CSV and dictionary formats require flat.
Roots depend only on names, kinds and file hashes of the exact prepared or downloaded retained data ZIP. Build version, label, Release repository/tag/asset and legacy VERSION advertisement bind separately in projcli.github-tree-snapshot.v1. No ordinary file data is stored as CAS objects. The complete readable history is deliberately retained beside the graph; this is a metadata trade-off, without a size or speed claim.
All bundle members are bounded and allowlisted. Every directory object’s ID is verified, and each tree binding must reconstruct the recorded inventory hash. Missing/corrupt nodes fail before HTTP publication. Existing flat bindings remain readable with unchanged IDs; switching styles retains compatible history and old nodes. New snapshots never destructively reinterpret an earlier format.
Prepare required graphs, history, bindings and data ZIPs before HTTP writes. Upload data and compatibility metadata, then the new metadata bundle. After all required target HTTP operations succeed, write all selected project full copies, then small references. Failures may leave earlier remote/full metadata effects; there is no atomic multi-target transaction. Ordinary restore still uses its compatible CSV/VERSION path and data ZIP, rather than treating these bindings as native CAS snapshots.


Legacy CAS name-list definitions keep their existing encoding and index schema. Their writer now claims the store and the separate project .projr lookup scope. Exact repeated version/label/digest rows are not appended again; earlier bytes and differing rows remain intact.
